utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: First, we will check everything. One moment, please. Is the interpretation coming through loud and clear? Can you hear me? Prosecutor, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Registrar? My colleagues? The assistant? All the staff, can you all hear me? Good morning. Good morning, Prosecutor. Perhaps we can continue with the testimony which we had to stop yesterday? Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. We would recall to the stand Captain Rechner. CAPTAIN PATRICK RECHNER, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Captain, can you hear me? But as you are a globe trotter, I am sure you will have no difficulties. Please proceed, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Captain Rechner, when we ended the day yesterday your were talking about a meeting you had with Koljevic, I believe, on May 29th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, May 29th is when we tried to arrange the meeting through his secretary when I was at my accommodations. The meeting actually took place finally on 15th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: OK. On June 15th. At that meeting he made a comparison comparing the taking of the hostages to the use of electric shock; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, and as an analogy of electric shock therapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What were the topics you discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My primary concern was just to raise some of our problems of the treatment we had incurred with him, and also discuss the future working relationship when the UN military observers and the Bosnian Serb government.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you raise with Mr. Koljevic the fact that you had been singled out of your observation team and the subject of allegations that you had been observers for the air strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, among the different topics discussed relating to future possibilities of UNMOs working on Bosnian Serb territory was the problem of security. I mentioned to him the fact that the local media had singled my team out, including me personally, as well as the Czech officer, Captain Zidlik, as being the ones responsible personally for guiding in the NATO air strikes. I mentioned to Professor Koljevic that those allegations would have to be withdrawn formally and publicly otherwise our security would be untenable on the Bosnian Serb side, because a lot of the local people, no doubt, would have believed the propaganda and would, perhaps, decide to take their revenge on us at some later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What was Koljevic's response to that request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not answer that question or my concern directly, but he mentioned that because of the magnitude of the crisis between the Bosnian Serb authorities and the UN, as a result of the NATO bombing, a completely new working relationship would have to be established between the UN and the Bosnian Serb authorities. I had asked him also whether we would be released to our office in Pale or evacuated to Belgrade like the other hostages had been. He mentioned no, everybody would be evacuated to Belgrade. That was the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did he talk about his perception of the air strikes and why it was necessary to take hostages in his mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I said, he mentioned that this crisis was of an extremely high magnitude and he referred to previous air strikes as well as the air strikes on the first day which was 25th May, and saying that in the past air strikes were not a problem. They were a token response by the UN where usually the Serbs would have some prior notice and/or the UN would strike a very small target without causing any significant damage. So, he mentioned that in the past it was not really a problem. The Serbs would understand once an air strike was conducted on a limited scale that the UN was prepared to escalate things. However, he mentioned the bombing on 26th May was completely out of proportion to the previous bombings and was extremely serious and endangered any future working relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: How did your meeting with Mr. Koljevic end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On a basically friendly note. He mentioned that we should have been released a bit earlier, but that there were some technical difficulties and we would be released very shortly, just to be patient for a couple of more days. Then he asked if we needed any food or anything. I mentioned the food was not the greatest, but it was military food and we understood. The only concern I had with him was that all the UN military observers who were detained with me get a chance to make a call, a telephone call, to their next of kin. He just noted it but did not mention whether or not he could do anything to grant us the detail or the right to make telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Just as a reminder to the court, what position did Koljevic hold in the Republika Srpska at the time this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic was the Vice President of Republika Srpska and also the Chairman of their State Committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What happened after this meeting with Koljevic on 15th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This meeting took place at the military police headquarters in the town of Pale, so I was taken back to the barracks right after the meeting, that is, the military barracks where we were being detained, so returned back to be with the rest of the military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When were you eventually released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on the afternoon of 18th June. That is, I say "released", that is when we were loaded on the buses in Pale and driven to Novi Sad in Vojvodina which is an area of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Before you were loaded on to the buses on June 18th, did you make an attempt to recover some of the equipment that you had in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had all been permitted on the morning of 18th June to go back to our accommodations and take our personal belongings. Because of several visits that we had managed to conduct with our guards to our accommodations, and as well the observers from the other teams were able to make visits to their accommodations, we noticed that a lot of personal things and UN equipment had been either stolen or confiscated by the Bosnian Serb Army or private individuals. So, naturally, we were concerned about the security of our office equipment. We knew or we presumed that the soldiers would try to do everything to prevent us from taking it. So we had actually too much to take anyway, so we had decided to only take some of the key items that would make the remaining equipment inoperable. So, in our team's case, we decided to take the antenna to our INMARSAT telephone, and also the hand set for the INMARSAT telephone and a short or a small blue box which is the transeiver for our CAPSAT which is another satellite communications means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: What occurred when you went to the office to try to recover these items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had managed to surreptitiously to take the items. I had managed to get the hand set to the INMARSAT telephone and leave the accommodations with it. However, Captain Zidlik, the Czech UNMO in my team, was still there and the landlady, Mrs. Mira Savic, went upstairs and noticed that the INMARSAT antenna was missing. She assumed immediately that we had taken it. So she turned to the Czech officer, was very angry, called him "an enemy of the Serb people", reported to the guard that we had taken some of the office equipment. The guard searched Captain Zidlik's belongings, found the INMARSAT antenna and also the transeiver to the CAPSAT system. However, the guard did not know what the CAPSAT transeiver was and asked Captain Zidlik what it was. So Captain Zidlik responded that it was just a personal item required for his telephone. The guard accepted that. Unfortunately, one of our interpreters, Svetlana Babovic, turned to the guard immediately and told him, "No, no, this is actually part of their CAPSAT or satellite communications system that they are trying to make their way with". She also mentioned at that time that the hand set to the INMARSAT telephone was missing and that, obviously, I had taken it because it was not in Captain Zidlik's belongings. So we were forced to return all these items.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you make any other efforts to acquire these items after they had been taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is all we could do. The only other thing I can mention is I was forced to come back to our accommodations and return the hand set. At that time our landlord, Mr. Danilo Savic, was there. He was very angry and we had a bit of an argument. Mr. Savic either, I think it was at that time, mentioned that he would immediately call Mr. Krajisnik, who is the speaker of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and report this what, according to him, was a terrible act on our part in trying to take our own communications equipment, so that would be reported to the Bosnian Serb authorities. I was then returned back to the barracks where we had been detained throughout the 24 days and a short time afterwards, I would estimate about 30 minutes, I received a telephone call from Professor Koljevic who apologised for the incident with the guards and our landlord about our communications equipment, and said he understood perfectly our concern about the security of our equipments and that Mr. Krajicnik had informed him of all the details, but wanted me to understand that it was necessary for them to keep all the equipment in the office and have it functioning because they needed to communicate with the UN, and that was their only reliable means. So they mentioned that they would continue using our interpreters, which were Bosnian Serb civilians, to operate the equipment in our office in order or to continue communicating with the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you ever get the equipment back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the equipment was there. I found subsequently talking over the next few months with some of my military observer friends that the equipment was left there and the interpreters continued to work alone in our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: When you were eventually taken to the buses to be removed from Pale, was there anyone there that talked to the hostages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just before being released, early in the afternoon of 18th June, Professor Koljevic came over and addressed, first, all of the Canadians, which was myself, plus 12 soldiers from the Canadian battalion in Viseko, and the other 14 military observers. In both instances, he apologised for the fact that we were detained, noting that when he had done his military service he had also spent sometime in a Yugoslav military jail so he understood some of the hardships of our detention. But he also mentioned, basically, the same thing as we discussed in our meeting on 15th June, that we should understand that this whole incident with the bombing was a terrible crisis between the UN and the Bosnian Serb authorities, and that the Bosnian Serbs authorities needed to send a strong signal to the UN. He reiterated the analogy of the electric shock, saying in some cases an electric shock can kill a patient, but in other cases it can cure him. That was the response or the magnitude of the response that they had chosen in order to send a signal to the UN about how upset they were about the bombing. He asked us to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: After you left Pale, where were you and the other hostages taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Novi Sad in the Vojvodina area of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Did you eventually make your way to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we spent the night in Novi Sad at a hotel, and then the next morning on 19th June we were driven to the airport in Belgrade and flown from there on a UN aircraft back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Have you been back to Pale since you were taken hostage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we have two very brief video clips that we would like to show. If we could have the lights dimmed and those two clips shown, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I said, those were very brief but, Captain Rechner, could you please comment on those two video clips?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one was a clip of Major Janusz Kalbarczyk who was the polish military observer, as I explained yesterday, that was first chained at the bunkers 300 metres away from us where the ammunition was exploding. It was with Major Kalbarczyk later in that day that we were taken blindfolded to the radar site at Jahorina. The image that you saw was the interview that the local Serb journalists conducted with him as he was handcuffed to the radar dome. The second image is a picture of me shortly after I was handcuffed around the lightning rod in front of the bunkers Jahorinski Potok on 26th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that concludes our testimony. We would tender the video as exhibits and open up the session for questions from the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecutor. I will ask my fellow Judges to put their questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Captain Rechner, could you tell to the court the specific role of the UN military observers in Pale during 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that the UN military observers in general or just my liaison team?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: No, in general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general, in Pale, the observers from what I called Sierra Echo 1, that is the normal observing team, their job was to control or verify the weapons held in the weapons collection points around Sarajevo, and also work on the front lines of the Bosnian Serb positions to monitor conflict activity, and report to directly through their headquarters to the UN Security Council on what the situation on the ground was, and also with respect to any violations of the cessation of hostilities agreement that was signed on 31st December 1994 between all the warring factions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The job of my liaison team was more of an administrative and political nature. We were the communications link between the Bosnian Serb military and political authorities and the UN headquarters, and on occasion as well we were used by some of the international aid or humanitarian organisations. So, in Pale, my team was responsible for communicating letters either by telephone or by fax to the Bosnian-Serb authorities and also sent their letters either by telephone or fax back to our military observers headquarters in Sarajevo. On occasion also we would hold some meetings to discuss problems that pertained to military observers. As I mentioned, the meeting at the beginning of May where we were trying to get some freedom of movement for our military observers to be able to leave the enclaves in the eastern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you did not have freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At the beginning, that is, from the end of December until, I would say, the middle of April, in Pale, that is moving around Pale, and also going to Sarajevo was no problem, but then the Bosnian Serbs placed severe restrictions on us where we had to request 48 hours in advance to be able to leave Pale and go into Sarajevo, for example. Then at the end we were basically under house arrest. We were not even allowed to leave the area of our residence at all. As far as the other military observers, such as the ones working in the safe areas of Srebrenica or Gorazde or Zepa, they did not have any freedom of movement outside of those areas, so any time they wanted to leave the enclaves or have some UNMOs go to the enclaves, they would have to send a message to us and we would gain permission or try to gain permission for them to move through the Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Captain Rechner, how long did you stay handcuffed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about six hours or five-and-a-half hours.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you attached to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To that pole, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it in any way, did it present any dangers for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say certainly, we were concerned about our safety from the point of any civilians trying to attack us. I mentioned yesterday the problem that when we were held up at the entrance to a bunker complex that a crowd of civilians had gathered and one of the individuals had assaulted me and then tried to shoot us. We were concerned at being left all alone attached to the bunkers or the lightning rods in front of them that some of these people may try to make their way to us and shoot us. The other danger, of course, was from any potential NATO air strikes because we were in front of one of the bunkers filled with ammunition that had not been hit yet, and we knew it was full of ammunition because the door was open and Captain Zidlik was able to see that there were some mines and mortar shells. Later on, one of the guards actually took a box of mortar shells and put it in front of Captain Zidlik to make him more comfortable so he could sit it on. I do not think it made Captain Zidlik very comfortable, but certainly the danger was there that if there was any resumption of bombing that any collateral damage could kill us. Then third problem was that, as I mentioned this Lieutenant Colonel who was filming us yesterday mentioned that even if the air strikes did not kill us that he would come by and shoot us at the end of the day. Also we were afraid if there was any NATO air strikes in other locations, that they may come by and start executing us one at a time to get the bombings stopped as they had threatened to do when they were in our office initially to get the bombings stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: At no stage did the authorities of Pale take measures to ensure your safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, like I mentioned, the two groups of delegations that visited us, including Mr. Zametica, did not make any efforts with the soldiers to get us released or moved to any location. They just walked by, took a look at us and, in Mr. Zametica's case, he even seemed quite content with the response of the military and had added that he was curious what General Smith would do now that they had taken us all hostage and used us as human shields in front of their strategic or important places.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So you used the "human shields", that is what they were after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think he used the word "human shields".

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But it was a description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in my case I felt as a human shield most certainly, because we were placed there to prevent any NATO air strikes from occurring.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Apart from using you, as you said, as human shields, were you subject to any ill-treatment? Were you mistreated by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly, no, but it depends what you call, how you define "ill-treatment", physically no. But the problem was that we were not allowed to make any contact with our next of kin. We had immediately requested to see representatives of the International Committee of the Red Cross who had an office in Pale and we knew all the members in the Red Cross office. That visit with the Red Cross, or that meeting with the Red Cross, did not take place until, I believe it was, 11th June. We had also requested to see a doctor because a lot of us were affected by the whole stressful nature of the ordeal. The visit of medical authorities did not take place, I think, until the ninth day of our hostage taking, so sometime around 5th June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain Rechner, I would like to ask you a question on the feelings you had when you were taken as hostage. I will not go back to all your statements and explanations -- you have done that well -- but military function is the honour, that is what is a driving force for you. Did at any point of time, as a military, as an officer, you feel humiliated in that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very much so, and I would say that this sense of humiliation and betrayal is what I guarded most from the whole experience. In our case, this aspect of humiliation and betrayal was particularly acute. Because of the nature of our work, we were the liaison team to the Bosnian Serb government and also the military High Command, so in the absence of any political, official political recognition of their governments, we were the closest thing that they had to any official international representation. I would say that our working relationship had been professional and good, and the fact that I had met Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic before when I was invited to a social function -- it was 9th January, their St. Stephen's Day celebrations -- and also the fact that we had done a lot of personal work, in particular, with the local hospital in getting some urgent medications to them to treat individual cases which we think saved people's lives, we thought we had good working relationships with the local community and their government, and we thought that our humanitarian work had been valued; and the fact that they had chosen to take us hostage, not only chosen us as hostages, but to begin with us and threaten to kill us or use us as human shields, was the most terrible part of the whole experience. I do not want to underestimate or devalue the concern we had for our own security because that was very real as well. On the first day I would say there were five clear instances where I thought I would lose my life, but this sense of betrayal and humiliation was also very, very strong.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you go so far as to say that deep down you felt that you had a role very similar to that as of a minister who with a white flag wants to talk about armistice and wants to negotiate in a position where you cannot be taken as a hostage? Do you see your situation as similar to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN military observers were working on the Serb side with the approval of the Serb authorities. We were unarmed, living in the local communities. We were there in order that we could report any cease-fire violations from the other side, that is, in the Sarajevo area from the Muslim forces to the UN. So our work was of direct value to the Serbs and they appreciated that and wanted us to work on their territory. In the case of our liaison team, they had requested our presence initially, and that is it was at their request that we were set up in Pale. Also, I found out shortly after I was released that the Bosnian Serb authorities had asked the UN military observer headquarters in Sarajevo if they could again send some military observers to Pale, because it was very important that they have a liaison team on the ground in Pale with which to deal.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I want to ask you a last question which is a marginal one but, nevertheless, deals with your stay in Pale: what impression did you have of that government, of the administration in Pale? We read a lot of things, there have been a lot of descriptions. You were a living witness of that government, of the administration there, of that corner on a hill in Sarajevo which is a self-proclaimed autonomous unit. What is your general feeling of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one was that they were very mistrustful of any foreigners, which included us. Unfortunately, for that reason we did not have as much direct access to the senior leaders and to work with them directly as one would normally expect. Our day-to-day working relationships was only with, which concerns, for example, Dr. Karadzic's office, with his secretary, Mira, and with his spokesman and political advisor, Mr. Zametica. In the case of Professor Koljevic, towards the end, he became a bit more open and I was able to discuss directly with him some of the problems, but normally I would deal with his secretary, Ceca. On the military side, partly because their headquarters were 60 kilometres away, we dealt normally only by telephone and fax machines, primarily through Colonel Milos Durdjic, who was their Senior Liaison Officer to the UN. His official functional or post was the head of the Bosnian Serb Army department for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations. But it is difficult for me to comment on the workings of the governments or on the personalities because of this barrier that they had put in font of them which prevented our access to them. But, as far as on a democratic level, there was no political opposition in Pale, no freedom of the press that we were able to see. So everything was very tightly controlled by the government. At the same time, because we knew a lot of people in the local community, the local people also, however, put their firm trust in their leadership, as far as I could tell. There were some small sentiments of displeasure over certain aspects of some of their policies but, in general, the people supported their military leaders. When asked about the lack of any democratic, political processes or freedom of press, the local people would answer that that was normal because they were at war and in wartime you need a strict authoritarian government in place.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. I have no further questions. The Tribunal would like to thank Captain Rechner for having appeared here on behalf of the Prosecutor. After having thanked you once for your clarity, I would like him to be accompanied out of the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel, before moving on to the next aspect that you will be outlining for us, the court would like to have a translation of the conversation Mr. Karadzic had on the hillside above Sarajevo when the sniping was taking place, the shelling. This was in the video that we saw. It was the writer or the Russian poet. There is a conversation there that goes on for quite a while which is in English, if I understood rightly, but he is speaking very fast. I would ask that in the case file we include the French translation of that conversation and the English transcription of it as well, of course. So, if you would be so good, we would like to see that. Thank you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We will take care of that request right away. Your Honour, this concludes our evidentiary presentation on the first indictment that is at issue in this Rule 61 hearing. We will now be proceeding with an evidentiary presentation for the second indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. We will be first calling Jean Rene Ruez as our witness. He will be a summary witness to describe the events relating to the indictment. We have prepared for your Honours copies of exhibit books. I would usher the ask, please, to present them to the court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel, will we be coming back to the documents in these files -- this is just a practical question -- because if we do not need these any more? OK. We will keep them up here. MR. JEAN RENE RUEZ, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good morning sir. First, if you would be so good as to read the declaration. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare I will tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Please be seated. Now your presentation will be under the guidance of counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Rene, please state your name and spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Jean Rene Ruez, R-U-E-Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you employed by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before being employed by the Office of the Prosecutor, can you inform the court of what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the judicial police in France. I have worked there for 10 years. I worked in Paris and Marseilles and I was in charge of a unit in Nice. That was my last position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long have you been employed at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been working for the Office of the Prosecutor since April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that capacity have you conducted an investigation into the events surrounding the takeover of Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour. I am not hearing the translation of my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are having translation problems? Can you hear the Presiding Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am all right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can hear the Presiding Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: To be sure that you also hear your witness, Mr. Harmon, so please go ahead. So can everyone hear in the public gallery? Can you hear the proceedings? Fine. So please go right ahead, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, when did you start your investigation into the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigation began in Tuzla on 21st July 1995. The first possibility to go in the Republika Srpska was on 21st January 1996, and since then several missions have been carried out in the relevant places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about the background events that led to Srebrenica becoming a UN safe area. Could you please describe those events, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be brief on this, in so far as it starts with the offensive on the enclave, that is what the investigation begins with. Generally speaking, since 1991/92, the region was subject to very high tension between the two communities there. There have been aggressions on both side. Towards mid '92, the people in the surrounding villages, given the aggression that was being carried out against them, had to flee and people gathered around the enclave. In late '92, early '93, the Bosnian Serb Army launched an offensive on these refugees in the enclave. The humanitarian conditions were awful there. There were air lifts to supply the people there. When the offensive was going full scale, General Morillon took action there and the offensive was stopped until April 1993 when resolution 819 was adopted by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, just a moment. Your Honours, Exhibit No. 1 that is in your binders are copies of the relevant UN resolutions here prepared. Mr. Ruez, what was the result of resolution 819?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Ruez and Mr. Harmon, to interrupt, but there is a map, maybe Mr. Ruez could indicate. I think I know where Srebrenica is, but I think it might be good just to explain a bit more the area that is involved. You mentioned the villages. Then maybe just very briefly if you could indicate on the map where those villages are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was my next question, as a matter of fact. I am going to refer to Exhibit No. 59 and Exhibit No. 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do apologise. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, would you, please, then refer to Exhibit 59 and Exhibit No. 2 and indicate for the court where the safe area was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The safe area is here near the Serbian border to the east, northeast of Sarajevo, to the north of the Zepa enclave. Now, on this map here, this is a blow-up of the region I have just indicated on the map, the safe area is in blue here. The red line is the confrontation line between the Bosnian Serb Army and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, the border runs along the river. It is the Drina. That is the border with Serbia to the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, how was resolution 819 implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 8th May '93 there was a demilitarisation agreement signed between the parties; the UN Battalion was assigned for protecting the enclave. Now, that agreement was never abided by by any party and UN UNPROFOR spent a lot of time trying to sort things out, both with the Bosnian Serbs and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me focus your attention in regard to the stationing of a battalion of peacekeepers to the enclave. When did the Dutch Battalion go into the enclave, Mr. Ruez? Is that in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in February 1994, a Dutch Battalion replaced the Canadian Battalion that was stationed within the enclave. The situation did not change. The agreement was not abided by. There were offensives being launched against the enclave by the Bosnian Serb Army that regularly bombarded -- bombed the enclave, and there were raids on the part of the Bosnian Army from inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the actual invasion of the enclave, was there a Bosnian Serb blockade of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the offensive started with a blockade. The convoys were no longer allowed to enter into enclave which gave rise to big problems when it came to humanitarian aid supplies. By way of an example, a kilo of coffee cost 80 Deutschemarks at the time. The blockade also had effects when it came to rotating the staff of the Dutch Battalion. They had quite some problems and, no doubt, the Dutch witness will be able to elaborate on that. Also, at the time there were some reinforcing of the Bosnian Serb Army around the enclaves, so one could assume that there was going to be an assault on the safe area in the near future.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please explain when the invasion began and describe what happened in the initial phases of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So then the invasion as such began on 5th July 1995, in the night of the 5th/6th July, some Bosnian Serb soldiers entered the enclave. There was more and more pressure on the enclave. The observation posts that had been set up by the Dutch Battalion were under fire. A number of posts, they were falling one after the other. The people there were caught in the cross-fire. The Bosnian Army also used the observation posts in response to the firing from the Bosnian Serb Army. The hostages or Dutch hostages were taken to assembly points. Their equipment was taken from them. On the whole, on the basis of the information we have, the people were treated relatively well. A team of cameramen filmed them while they were in the custody of General Mladic's forces. The villages in the environs were being bombed more and more regularly, more and more intensely. The people there had to flee and they moved into Srebrenica and gathering there, awaiting an intervention on the part of NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please describe for the court the significant events that occurred in the enclave on July 10th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The day before, that is to say, 9th July, the UN sent in ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs troops calling for the withdrawal of their troops from the enclave by 6 a.m. the next morning, otherwise there would be air strikes. Now, the following day, on 10th, the attack continued. There was bombing. The people who were in the environs of Srebrenica all sought refuge within the town. Now, what they had to decide is how to react to events. On 10th, some of the male population decided to flee through the woods towards Tuzla. Now, the Dutch Battalion -- that is in Srebrenica but it is Potocari that it has its main compound -- were getting ready for a massive inflow of refugees. In Potocari, they were getting things ready because they were expecting some 25,000 people to be coming in and they were expecting them from one moment to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was reaction of General Mladic to the UN ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reaction of General Mladic to that ultimatum, well, was in turn an ultimatum. The Bosnian Army was given 24 hours to surrender. Also, the Dutch Battalion was given an ultimatum not to allow any refugees within the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to the refugees who had been in the enclave, the city of Srebrenica, around the Dutch B COY unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 11th July, subsequent to the ultimatum from Mladic, the crowd gathered in Srebrenica at the Dutch compound B COY, is what it is referred to. People gathered there right from the morning, waiting for the air raids that were supposed to take place. There were some 15,000 people at Srebrenica at the time gathered there in front of the compound. The crowd tried to get inside, managed to get inside and then the ultimatum from the day before goes into effect and three shells land within the compound among the people. We do not how many people were hurt or killed, because there is an outbreak of panic amongst the crowd and people are running towards Potocari. The evacuation of the hospital takes place around 11 o'clock that morning. The people are fleeing under the bombs, the roads being bombed all along its way, that is, from -- we are talking about four kilometres, from Srebrenica to Potocari. Once they got to Potocari, the people are gathered around the Dutch compound. People are left within it, but quite quickly the situation becomes unbearable. The compound is invaded, as it were, by the crowds. There is not enough room to let everyone in. The people are directed towards other areas, towards factories in the neighbourhood. This is an industrial area you have around Potocari. The firing goes on. There are several shells that land around the compound and people have to seek shelter within the factories there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I would like to go back to the shelling of the B COY compound in the city of Srebrenica. Who fired those shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb Army shelled B COY.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did air strikes occur on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were air strikes late in the morning. While the people were fleeing towards Potocari, there was an air strike then that was carried out. The soldiers, the Muslim soldiers, who were there could see what the result of the firing was. Seeing that the strikes were not what they had hoped for, that the result was not such as it would make the Bosnian Serb Army retreat, the military leaders decided to evacuate the army, the Muslim army, from Srebrenica. So, people took two different directions, women, elderly, children, fled towards Potocari; men, the fit to serve men, who did not want to fall into the hands of the Bosnian Serb Army, headed for the woods. They gathered in a village near Potocari, Susnjari, and from there they all gathered and all the other men started coming in, getting ready to all head out together. A lot of civilians followed the soldiers and so they set up shop there waiting for night fall to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the air strikes occurred, what was General Mladic's reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The immediate reaction of General Mladic was to threaten the Dutch Battalion, saying that he would do away with the Potocari compound. They had the military means to do so. There were some heavy artillery stationed around there. There were multiple rocket launchers, tanks, mortars and the threat was also to kill the hostages. I do not know how many hostages there were, but there were 55 hostages in the Dutch Battalion and there were interpreters there who told them what those threats were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in the city of Srebrenica after the population fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we know what happened in Srebrenica -- Drazen Erdemovic, he confessed, he is a Bosnian Serb soldier who is in custody with the Tribunal. Now, that day when people left the city, the first Bosnian-Serb forces entered Srebrenica. Everyone had not left. There were a number of civilians who were still in the town. All of those civilians were gathered on the Srebrenica soccer field. Drazen Erdemovic does not know what happened on the soccer field, the fate of the people there is not known. We have lost trace of them. Now, what can be said is that at least one person was killed in cold blood on that occasion because he saw that. He says that there was a murder committed against a Muslim civilian there at Srebrenica, so on orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the night of July 11th, did General Mladic meet with the Dutch Commander of the UN peacekeepers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a meeting at Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel. General Mladic and General Zivanovic met with Colonel Karremans. They met twice on that day. The fate of the hostages and the people was discussed. Since there is going to be another witness discussing this, there is no point in me elaborating on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ruez, I would now like to turn your attention to 12th July 1995. Can you please describe to the court what happened in relation to the column of men who had fled into the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 15,000 men had gathered at Susnjari on 11th in the evening. The column started fleeing towards Tuzla, following the line here that I am indicating on the map. Now, to do that they had to first go through the minefields that had been set up all around the enclave. They left towards 11.00, 11 p.m. It was a very slow process because people had to go in single file. There was about a metre wide track through the minefields so it was quite difficult going. During the night, the column was not subjected to any attacks really, so it was a rather quiet night. But, as of the morning, that is to say, when the column was about 15 kilometres long, the first bombing occurred. The column was ambushed on several occasions. Several bombings took place. So the army was in the lead; so the military forces were in the front; the civilians were in the middle and in the rear mixed with a few soldiers who were there to oversee their protection on the flanks. All kinds of weapons were used to fire at the columns, from anti-aircraft guns to others, mortars. The Bosnian Serb troops who were mainly stationed there along this strategic road, and so there was no possibility to flee towards Tuzla along this road. A lot of witnesses referred to the fact that there were people along there and there were also UN people along there. Blue helmets were there. Promises had been made. They had been given assurances. Several witnesses said this, that people were told that in case they surrendered etc., they did not even fear for their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Ruez, that there was a Bosnian Serb military presence along the road. Could you please point to the court where the trap line was set?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main military presence is on the road here that is in red on the map, and so that is in the way of the way they wanted to flee. The main ambush took place above Kamenica. When the column of refugees was massively concentrated at that point, there was a severe ambush that has been described by a number of witnesses. People were surrounded. They tried to flee and they were mowed down there. A lot of them were killed. The bodies are still there. A lot of journalists have gone there and seen that a lot of bodies are still there, corpses; amongst them military people as well as a large number of civilians. Towards 6 p.m. on the road, the Army managed Nova Kasaba, at about the height there. So right after they got through, there was a second ambush that occurred and the civilian population that was trying to get through at that time could not get through. Everybody was held up afterwards and the group started breaking up in so far as possible, just a total chaos. Various groups of different sizes of 30, 100,000 people are looking for some way to get out of that area. Now, groups are captured. One witness reports the arrest of a group of about 65 people, half of them are immediately killed and the rest taken to unknown places. There are a number of scenes that are referred to that take place during the night. One prisoner who was hiding in the woods, observed the capture of another who was immediately tortured. He had his nose and ears and lips cut off before he had his throat slit. A number of witnesses also described the infiltration of the column by Bosnian Serb soldiers who, taking advantage of the cover of darkness, mixed in with the crowd, gave people faulty directions, directed them towards areas where there were ambushes or directed them towards the Bratunac/Nova Kasaba road where the Army was waiting for them, and you can imagine what happened when they got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Ruez, can you describe whether or not there was a meeting in Bratunac on the morning of 12th July between General Mladic and the representatives of Dutch BAT unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a meeting did take place in the morning at Bratunac. General Mladic had asked the day before the Dutch Colonel to come with representatives of the Muslim population. Now, all of the representatives had already taken off the first part of the column, as I said earlier, that managed to get through, was made up of civilians -- some civilians, mainly military people and also the spouses of a number of people of the municipality. So they had all gone. Several representatives were called on. These are not professional representatives, if I might say so; these are people who agreed to stand in as representatives. There was a woman amongst them as well as a man, Ibro Nuhanovic. In the course of the meeting -- Colonel Karremans will no doubt have some comments on this -- Ibro Nuhanovic told his son when he came back that General Mladic had asked that the men of 17 to 65 years old be questioned to see whether they have committed any war crimes during the previous period. You will be hearing more about that from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to focus your attention on Potocari, the UN compound there, particularly on the morning of July 12th. Can you describe to the court what was occurring at that compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 12th July, the Bosnian Serb Army reached Potocari. The night had been quiet. People had gathered in the factories. Everyone was very concerned about what was going to be happening the following day. In the morning, the people saw that some houses were on fire in the environs of Potocari. The first troops entered the city and immediately asked the blue helmets to hand over their equipment. They take away the bulletproof vests. They take away their helmets. They mixed with the people. The refugees talked to these people and realised that they are not Dutch, that they are Serbian, and they realised what a terrible situation is developing. These soldiers start handing out candy to children and asking questions about the army, where the army is, where have the men gone. The meeting that is taking place at that time in Potocari between General Mladic and the Dutch Commander is not yet over, and there is already a large number of trucks showing up in Potocari. Everybody is quite surprised by the number of vehicles that turned up. Now, shortly after the trucks arrived, General Mladic turns up at Potocari and he talks to the crowd. He explains to the people that they are going to be evacuated, that nobody is going to harm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, have you prepared some film footage about what you have just testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please describe what the court will be seeing on the film footage that we are about to play?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we are just about ready to have a recess, so maybe we could work our recesses in consistent with the testimony, so it is up to you to say. Do you think we should proceed to a recess now or do you think that we should first watch the video that has been prepared by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could play the video -- it is not long, your Honour -- it would be a guide of good time to break right after the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. So, please proceed, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards this video, there is a choice of scenes. At first, you will see the crowd gathered in front of the Srebrenica UN compound. That is on the 10th, that is to say, the day before the invasion. Now, as regards the quality of the film, it is quite frankly not all that good. Then there are going to be some excerpts from Serbian television showing very briefly the attack on the city. Then there will be a few scenes about showing the air strikes. Then there is going to be a clip with Mladic at Srebrenica. Then there will be a view of Potocari, but this is prior to the events showing where things are located, the factories. Then you will see the arrival of the refugees on 11th in the morning and, lastly, you will see General Mladic at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could lower the lights, please, and play Exhibit 3, clip No. 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So, I said it is not very good, but there are groups of men, women and children here who have assembled before the compound. People are wondering what is going to happen to them, and it is here that the following morning the shells would be landing in the midst of the crowd. There there is a group of men involved in a discussion. It was after that kind of a discussion that the men would decide to flee through the woods. At times the people are standing in the way of the UN vehicles, to keep them there so that they would not leave. Now, this was on Serbian television. These are scenes of the attack. This is an artillery commander who is directing the fire. The Bosnian Serb soldiers on the road south of the enclave. Then this relates to the air strikes there. General Mladic who is entering Srebrenica from the south. There are a few other Generals there. General Mladic gives the order to continue towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have had translated the words of General Mladic in the last segment of the film that you have seen. I would ask Mr. Ruez to please read the translation into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, thank you. That was the question I was going to put to you, that we include that in the case file, but you are saying that is the translation of the last bit of the film. We actually would prefer having all of the last clip, that is to say, from the moment on when General Mladic enters Srebrenica. So if we could have all of that at one point in time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is no problem, your Honour. Mr. Ruez, would you please read what I have asked you to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is just, what you refer to is he wanted to have removed a Muslim flag that had remained on a barricade. He asked that a picture be taken of it first. With regard to the other scenes, he congratulated his colleagues. He gave them the order to continue in the direction of Potocari. With regard to the brief interview he gave a journalist who was there and who had quite apparently been taken along in the operation, the text is the following: "There you go, Srebrenica on this 11th July 1995, a Serbian; just before another Serbian holiday we can offer this to the Serbian people. After the rebellion of the Dahijas, we can revenge the Turks in this area". The rebellion against Dahijas, that is a reference to an uprising of local officers under the Ottoman Empire and in 1804 there had been that uprising and there had been the slaughter of Serbian officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I think this is an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The clip was not finished. There was still a view of Potocari and the refugees there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We can come back to that after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until 11.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to read into the record again, returning to that film clip with General Mladic, the English translation of what he said, I quote: "Here we are in Srebrenica on July 11th 1995. On the eve of yet another great Serbian holiday we present this city to the Serbian people as a gift. Finally, after the rebellion against the Dajihas, the time has come to take revenge on the Turks in this region". When we broke, your Honour, we had two portions of the film that we still wanted to show, so if we could have the lights dimmed we will proceed with those portions of the film clip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This video was filmed from the roof of the main compound of Potocari. It gives you a general idea of the situation at that time. Here you have the road which goes to Potocari, on the right to Bratunac. There you have the surrounding hills with individual homes. Several factories are clumped together in the peripheral area. The film was taken before the events and at that moment there were no refugees. This is the type of factory where the population sought refuge and this is a view of the back of the factory. At 11 o'clock in the morning the first refugees arrived at Potocari. They were transported by truck, but the majority of the people fled on foot. The people are helped by Medicines sans Frontier and other people who helped them. A lot of people suffered casualties, were injured. What you should note, it was July and it was extremely hot. Here are other trucks which are arriving at the camp. Every space is used by the population so that they can flee as quickly as possible. Now, these are the news of the Serb Television describing the events, the arrival in Potocari. The situation on 12th in Potocari. Women refugees in Potocari. The first speech of General Mladic to the crowd -- afterwards there were many others. He is reassuring everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you have translated the words of General Mladic that are shown in that last film clip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a text here in English. When General Mladic talked to the crowd he said the following: "Do not be afraid. Just take it easy, easy. Let women and children go first. Plenty of buses will come. We will transfer you towards Kladanj". Kladanj which is here on the map, so you can see the road which was taken, for the deportation of the people. "From there you will cross to the territory controlled by Alija forces", this is referring to Alija Izetbegovic. "Just do not panic. Let women and little children go through first. Do not let any of the children get lost. Do not be afraid. Nobody will harm you", and the people thanked him. Then he gave an interview to a reporter who was present: "Today I received a delegation from the population and they asked me whether I could give them the means to help them leave the territory. They wanted to leave and cross the territory controlled by the Muslims and Croats. "Our Army does not want combat activities against civilians, nor against the UNPROFOR forces. The aim was not to fight civilian populations. We have nothing against the people here or UNPROFOR. We have provided transportation, food, water and medicine for them. During the day we are going to evacuate women and children, elderly persons and all others who are willing to leave this area of combat activities without being forced to do so". That was the interview with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, can you describe to the court what happened in Potocari after the arrival of General Mladic and the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of the interview with General Mladic, the soldiers surrounding him went to the crowd and separated the women and the men. Many men were still present in Potocari at that moment. Many of them did not want to leave their families; others also had family ties to remain there. Some did not want to have the risk of going through the woods. About 3,000 men were still in Potocari at that moment then. The deportation evacuations happened almost immediately. The people went to the buses. The Dutch soldiers tried to have some order and instil the order in the crowd. General Mladic also was in charge or controlled the evacuation and explained to everybody before they got into the bus that the men would follow on. The men who tried to get on the buses, some managed, others were immediately separated by the soldiers and taken out and taken to houses which were in the surrounding areas. Murder was done by two soldiers of General Mladic of a person, who of a man, who tried to get on to the bus. The soldiers in Potocari mixed in with the crowd and separated the men who were there with their families still. A witness who was there in the factory on 11th March saw several soldiers entering the factory. Some of them went towards a woman who had a baby in her arms, asked for the gender of the baby. The woman said it was a boy and immediately the soldier killed the baby with a knife. The mother fell unconscious and everybody tried to flee. The witness also left the site. Many bodies were seen without having any direct witness of what actually happened. Near a stream there were seven bodies lying down, and he noticed that all had their throats cut and one had the head severed almost completely from the body. There were about 10 other bodies behind the factory. Then there was another group of soldiers who were hiding behind a house. Two of their colleagues went towards the crowd that was gathering just in front of the factory, and pointed out the men and put them in small groups behind the factory. An opening was created so that the people could pass and go to the side away from the crowd. Men arrived in small groups of 10. About 20 soldiers were waiting for them and killed them with knives one after the other. There was no movement of revolt that was felt or seen. This lasted for several hours. The bodies piled up. Prisoners were made -- were ordered to put them in order. A truck arrived and they were loaded on to the truck. Those who had to do the work were then executed. There were about -- the trucks came about five times to collect the bodies and took them to an unknown destination. The soldiers gradually in the afternoon became more and more mixed in the crowd. Some were recognised by people whom they knew before these events took place. The United Nations soldiers were forced to give their materiel, for example, their helmets, their vehicles. The Serb soldiers got into the vehicles. Many men were separated and were taken to an unknown destination behind the houses. There are a lot of possibilities there in order to carry out mass executions. One heard shots coming from the area around the houses. A witness saw two men who were taken into a building, and some time later there were seven bodies found in this location. During the evacuation process one man was separated from his family. He was also killed with a knife by a soldier. There was panic in the crowd. People tried to clamber on to the buses, some managed to, and the separation process continued throughout the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, can you please describe the deportation process that first day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That afternoon, 12th July, 5,000 people were deported from Potocari to Kladanj. For the first group, the things happened relatively well or according to plan. The escorts who had accompanied the convoys had their people taken. The soldiers could not carry out their functions. Their vehicles were taken from them. On the route, the people saw groups of prisoners along the roadside. They saw abandoned bags, some bodies here and there scattered along the roadside in the area shaded in red on the map. A medical convoy was also evacuated in the direction of Kladanj. The convoy is stopped at Tisca which is the last stop before the confrontation lines, and the rest they had to do on foot. The prisoners left the trucks and were beaten. One prisoner had a number of fractures because he was kicked when he got out of the bus. The men in Potocari were also deported in the direction of Bratunac. Firstly, they were left in empty, abandoned houses. They were squashed into the houses. They were evacuated by bus as well and left in a hangar in Bratunac. During this process they did not mix with the rest of the crowd. They had buses specially for them. They went towards those buses in a column; no women were amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to Potocari that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once the deportation had taken place for the 12th, people sought refuge in the factories, but also outside the factories because the factories were crammed. During the night soldier groups continued to monitor them. They went amongst the people with electric torches and selected this or that man; they had to get up and follow the soldiers. Women were shouting when their husbands or children were taken. No-one really knew what was going on. Everyone was panicking. One witness who was just behind the factory noticed that groups of men were taken behind that factory of, say, 10 or 20 and the soldiers were waiting for them there. The prisoners were killed with a knife. There were hundreds of victims during that night. That was according to this particular witness. At the end of the evening in one of those factories soldiers who were going into the crowd separated the men out. They selected a family with three children. They separated the children from the mother who fell unconscious because she was so frightened. The three young men, about 11, 17 and 18, fell behind the factory. Then there was a group of women who appeared who wanted some news about what was happening behind the factory which was not lit and, therefore, no-one wanted to go there. They saw the three bodies of those young men who had been slit, their throats had been slit just behind the factory. The procedure continued throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation in Potocari on the morning of 13th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day the process continued. A witness saw two young girls taken from the factory, 11th of -- and then he saw their body, their throat was slit behind a building. During the night many people had, obviously, quite clearly, panicked and had been stopped and committed suicide. Their bodies were found hanging in the factory. Witnesses who were in that area in search of water noticed that the bodies were close to a river which was filled with blood. Women tried to look for water. In or near Potocari there are some water pumps behind the houses where people could get water. Near these water pumps there were also bodies who were slit, their throats were slit. There was a lot of blood around. One body was found hanging, according to one witness who was there at dawn who worked for the parking company, which was a bus company, there was a mutilated body that was found hanging. The nose was cut, the ears were cut off, the lips were cut off. Again near the river another witness saw 25 bodies who had been executed and all lying down. Bodies that were lying there were also confirmed by the Dutch soldiers. One of these soldiers saw nine bodies in a field behind the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the deportation process begin again on 13th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The process continued from 7 o'clock in the morning onwards. General Mladic said that the deportation would take place at 7 o'clock and, in fact, that did take place. Quite a few buses arrived. Then again murder was committed. Where as the crowd tried to come near to the buses, they were pushing on to each other because they saw what had happened in the evening and what the soldiers had done, so they were trying to get away as fast as possible from that area. One soldier approached a woman in the middle of the crowd who was trying to get on to a bus. Her child was crying. The soldier asked why the child was crying. She explained that he was hungry. The soldier made a comment saying, "Oh, well, the child will not be hungry any more" and slit the child's throat in front of everybody and then she tried to flee by getting on to a bus. The procedure of separation continued. It was more pressing than the day before. That was the 13th. Selection was very stringent. Men were put in the houses and were waiting for them to be transported but at a later stage so that they too would go to Bratunac where they would be put into an old school. On the route to Kladanj, the buses often stopped. Soldiers got on to check that there were no men hidden in the buses. Some men who were there were made to get out of the buses. Women were threatened. They were threatened, for example, if they did not hand over the money that they had or did not hand over all their possessions. Many prisoners were seen during the route along the roadside. They had to show three fingers which is a sign of victory for the Serbs. They were forced to sing songs. Some recognised their husband, their son amongst the prisoners. For the men who managed to remain on the buses, the last stop was at Tisca. That was the last point before the evacuation over the confrontation line. The men were removed from the rest of the refugees and taken to a school, the school in Tisca. During that day the deportation took place because 25,000 people were evacuated. 60 buses and trucks were used for the transportation of all these people. The buses belonged to a civil, local company. The drivers were also civilians. Some men managed, however, to get across the confrontation line, thanks in particular to the attitude of some of the drivers. The drivers did not all have the same attitude -- far from it. On that day, the civil negotiators were also evacuated. Everything happened well, according to them, for the negotiations on behalf of the women who were asked to represent her part of the population. Things were running smoothly. She was convinced that since she was selected as representative of the population, since she wanted to try -- she tried to commit suicide before getting on to the bus. People came to her. She had to get on to the bus. Then she saw her name on a list with a question mark in the hands of a Serbian soldier. She crossed the confrontation line at Kladanj. The third civil negotiator, Ibro Nuhanovic, left the Dutch compound with his wife and son. He was seen for the last time by a witness when he was trying to get on to a bus. He was beaten by Bosnian Serb soldiers. Since that time, his son, Hasan, is looking desperately for news from his family. The son has received no news whatsoever from his mother, from his father or from his other brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, could you please describe what happened to the column of men that had fled into the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night of the 12th to 13th was very, very difficult for the population who were fleeing into the woods. During the night these groups became more dispersed and tried to escape the ambushes waiting for them, but many were captured. At dawn a group, for example, was captured when they were trying to cross the tarmac road near Kasaba. They were captured. Along the road the prisoners saw a living body of a mutilated body. Again the nose, ears and lips were cut. It seems to be a common form of torture. The prisoners were put in Kasaba where they were put in an army barracks before being moved to the football stadium where many prisoners had gathered and were concentrated on that particular day. Another witness was in the forest away from the group and saw a group of soldiers approaching some injured people who had been abandoned because they could not be transported. They could not transported and taken by the refugees. All had their throats slit. They saw other bodies when they were trying to cross and moving and escaping, and they felt and think that the casualties and the injures were caused by shrapnel, and also injuries caused by knives and many of them again had their throats slit. Another group was captured near Nova Kasaba. The soldiers who captured them made some comments, were saying that the army was authorised to pass but the civilians were not allowed to pass. Civilian prisoners were taken apart, were separated from the rest. The majority of those people were immediately executed when they were detained. During that time other groups, who no longer knew what direction to take, heard the Bosnian Serbian army who were along the strategic route promising through loud speakers that they would help them, that they had the Red Cross, that nothing would happen to them, that the United Nations soldiers were there present, and they also saw blue helmets along the roadside, but they were not really the blue helmets; they were Bosnian Serbian soldiers who were using stolen materiel, in fact. A large group of prisoners which was surrounded in or near Kamenica went on to the tarmac route where they were taken over by the Bosnian Serbian soldiers. All those people were taken into a field which is in Sandici. They were asked to stay there and wait until something further happened to them, further instructions. One person expressed his dissatisfaction and he was immediately beaten by the soldiers and was killed. After some hours on that site in the field the prisoners were taken on foot in the direction of Kravica which is very close by. At Kravica, that entire group, there were about 500 to 1,000 individuals, were forced to enter into a hangar. The people were forced to sit down. When the last one entered into the hangar, there was not enough space for him to sit down. The soldiers ordered him to sit down and since he did not act fast enough, he was beaten. Immediately, the soldiers who were around the hangar fired into all the openings of the hangar. Grenades were thrown into the hangar. Those who tried to escape by the openings were beaten by the soldiers at the outside of the hangar. Once the smoke was in the hangar, the firing started again. After the firing the soldiers on the outside asked if there was anyone who still was alive, some answered. They were asked to leave the hangar and as soon as they left the hangar you heard shots on the outside of the hangar as well. Nevertheless, some people managed to survive from this execution which took place inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, have you visited that hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like now to show you Exhibits 4, 5, 6 and 7 and ask you to describe the significance of each of those to the court. Could we lower the lights, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the hangar at Kravica. It is on the right-hand side of the road. Just behind that there is a hill. It is a very hilly area all along that road, and the people tried to get away going over the hills. So that is the opening through which the prisoners went in, that is right there. But others were penned in the neighbouring parts. Now, the impacts here, do you see, from the bullets do not all come from that incident. There has been fighting going on here since 1992, so there has been some damage from other causes as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which exhibit is this one you are putting on the monitor, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us see. This is a photo that was taken inside the hangar near a window. Grenades had been thrown in through the windows and all of these spots you see here on the wall are blood. There was some sampling done on 21st January of this year and it was human blood. Other analyses have been carried out subsequently in the course of other missions there. Inside the hangar there were signs of gunshot all over, black, the walls are black from previous fire when there was a fire, but this was before that happened, but the bullet fire is quite clear. It is white against that black background. On this following photograph you can see on this wall human debris, if you will, that has been splashed on to the wall, and this is what you see throughout that hangar. On the inside all these human remains that have been splashed against the walls. The next photo this was the ceiling, from the ceiling which is about 3 metres high, or rather this is the ceiling, excuse me, and you can see the blood on this ceiling that is some 3 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right if we could have the lights, please. Mr. Ruez, would you please continue with your description of what happened to the people in the column that had fled Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other prisoners were captured. Some of them were not taken to the tarred road but stayed in the hills. Now a witness described the capture of a group that had been surrounded for a number of hours. The people were put in a circle. The BSA soldiers were around them. They started by taking a number of the individuals in the group and to execute them summarily. There is not just killing, there is also torture. Prior to the killing there was a woman who was slaughtered in front of everyone. There is a man who is accompanied by his young son and a soldier comes up to him, makes some comments about the fact that his father is in the process of killing off Serbian children. He takes the old man, puts the knife through his hand, sticks it to the tree, then cuts open the stomach of the little boy and then on the tip of the knife he has a bit of an organ from the inside of the child's stomach and then he forces the man to eat that part of the child's innards. A child is separated from its mother who is fighting with the two soldiers to try to get her son back. The son is thrown up and he is hit with bayonets before being beaten once he hits the ground. This process goes on the whole afternoon. The soldiers are taking their time. They are going around, the soldiers, picking up one or the other and executing them in front of everyone else. There as well there are in fact some survivors. There are other groups that are surrounded. There are a lot of suicides that are committed. Seeing what happens to people that are being detained, some people would rather commit suicide than fall into the hands of their enemies. A lot of people go mad, and suicides are being committed in a rather wild fashion. There are grenades that are let go, people are being hurt left, right and centre.
