utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very well. A last question I would like to ask, but perhaps it will also be part of your concluding statement. This is for the Prosecutor. In your opinion, was the main purpose of Srebrenica, was this, if there was any kind of a premeditated plan, and only the Tribunal will be able to determine that, was the physical elimination or deportation the main objectives as part of ethnic cleansing? Were both of these chosen without making a distinction or was deportation, expulsion, freeing of the territory given preference, and that these people were killed because there were logistical problems that arose at the last minute; or in your opinion -- I am asking you to give the opinion -- was the physical elimination part also of ethnic cleansing of that enclave as something being premeditated? Could you give us proof of that premeditation or would you prefer to talk about this as well in your concluding statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again I will talk about that in my concluding statement, but it is clear from the indictment that we have presented to the court that it is the Prosecutor's position that these killings amounted to genocide and they were part of the ethnic cleansing that took place throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; they being the final and, perhaps, most repulsive manifestation of that ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I do not have any further questions, nor do my colleagues. The only thing left for us to do is to thank our witness for the consistency and the clarity of his statement. I suggest that we suspend the hearing until 4.45. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (The court adjourned for a short time). (4.45).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. As our next witness we would like to call Colonel Karremans. While we are waiting for Colonel Karremans, your Honours, we will tender the Exhibits that were referred to by Mr. Ruez in his previous testimony. In regard to the large map with multi-coloured dots and markers on them, we propose to have a colour photograph taken of that large exhibit. We will preserve the large map and submit as part of the record the colour photographs of the map, if that is all right with the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor, the Tribunal accepts that evidence, all the documents, and accepts that a photograph of the map, according to the technical facilities we have, will be added. We have now Colonel Karremans before us. We will have to give limb some headsets. Can you hear me sir? Can you read the statement which you have in your hand? Can you please give Colonel Karremans some headsets? I think that you must give the headsets each time and the Usher should be told of that. Please read the statement which you have in your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Please be seated. Colonel Thomas Karremans, sworn.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, the Tribunal dealing with Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic wanted to call upon you here so that we can see what you have to say in the light of the indictment. I think it is the Office of the Prosecutor who will introduce you. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Colonel Karremans, could you place state your full name and spell your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My last is name is Karremans. I will spell that. K-A-R-R-E-M-A-N-S, Karremans. My first name is Thomas, T-H-O-M-A-S, and middle name Jacob.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My occupation now is that I am taking over an assignment in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Dutch Military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a member of the Dutch Military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you participate in UN peacekeeping operations in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you assigned in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was assigned in Bosnia-Herzegovina last year from January up to July in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in that particular assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mission was I was the Battalion Commander of Dutch BAT in the safe area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the UN mandate that you received in relation to your assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UN mandate for specially the safe havens or safe areas like Srebrenica was based on one of the United Nations' Resolutions, I can remember 819, after there was a cease-fire agreement between General Morillon and General Mladic in 1993. After that agreement the Canadians went in in the safe area and we took over a year after that in 1994. My assignment there was the Commander of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, did the Bosnian Serb Army interfere or obstruct with your Unit's ability to perform its mandate after you had arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not at the time that we arrived, but they did during our stay in the enclave during, let us say, the last five months, as of half February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you expand on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can expand on that, but then I have first, let us say, to explain what the mission was of the Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was two-fold. One was the purely military side of the mission and the other side was the humanitarian one. The military was to look to the cease-fire agreement between both warring factions of both parties, to assist the civil authorities in the opstina of Srebrenica, to maintain negotiations between the BSA and the BiH and, of course, trying to reject the BSA from attacking the enclave. On the other hand, the humanitarian side of the mission was to support the refugees within the enclave as much as possible on medical, by food, by, let us say, the infrastructure within in the enclave, to enhance that, and that was, let us say, the second part of the mission of the Battalion. When we took over in January 1995 from, let us say, the second Battalion, we were the third there, we had no problems during the rotation. We had no problems in the beginning with the BSA. There were some problems with the BiH, the Bosnian forces, in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What problems developed with the Bosnian Serb military? Can you describe those, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those problems started actually on 18th February when the last convoy came in with diesel, gas, which we needed for the performance of the mission. I can a little bit expand on that. Normally we used 4,000 to 5,000 litres a day for our vehicles for patrolling, for resupply of the observation posts, etc. As of 18th February the last diesel convoy came in, and that meant that we have to reorganise our mission, our work, because you need that amount of fuel for doing a mission. At the end during February, March, April up to July, the amount of diesel we had became less and less, and that meant that at the end we did our patrolling, and this is just one example, by foot. We were not able to resupply our observation posts. We were not able to do the patrolling by cars or combat vehicles. That meant we have to do all the patrolling by foot, with all the possible problems of the mining around and within the enclave. That was the example of diesel. At the end of April the real convoy terror, as we called it in those days, started because as of 26th April no convoy came in at all. That meant no personnel which was on leave in the Netherlands came back. They were stuck in Zagreb and they never returned. Under those persons, the military from our Battalion, about 180 at the end stuck up in Zagreb, there were some quite important persons. For instance, my Ops officer, a Major, most of the Deputy Company Commanders, and some other persons working in my battalion staff. That happened as of the end of April. That meant also that at the end of April, not allowing convoys coming in, that I had no resupply of medicines for the Battalion but also for the population, the refugees, within the enclave, no food supplies, no spare parts for my vehicles, the weaponry, no engineer equipment to assist the opstina and the people living in the opstina for repairs of the infrastructure, and no equipment to test my ammunition vehicles. That happened, let us say, until the last day I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What effect did this have on the civilian -- did the Bosnian Serb blockade have on the civilian population within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did, because almost, let us say, 25,000 persons living in the enclave were refugees, as there used to live about 8,000 in the village of Srebrenica. So you can imagine that the civil authorities had a mighty challenge to bring under all those refugees in a city with infrastructure for only 8,000 persons. But also the food for all the people living in the enclave was a problem, because the UNHCR was responsible, or at least they were responsible, for bringing in the food. Also the UNHCR had the same problems with getting in their food for the inhabitants of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were complaints made to the Bosnian Serb authorities about the blockade and its effects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir. Every day at 6 o'clock in the night we sent our information daily to the higher echelons and that started in sector northeast in Tuzla, going up to Sarajevo, the Bihac Command, up to the Force Commander in Zagreb. They were aware of, let us say, the problems within the enclave, on one side with the Battalion and on the other side with the population. We noticed that and we put all the information, let us say, on a daily basis to the higher echelons. On top of that I have written a lot of reports during my may stay over there, let us say, once in two days, in describing the poor situation of the people over there. Also after the meetings we had with the local authorities they always mentioned what their problems were towards the people. We mentioned that in our daily reports and I mentioned that quite some times in my, let us say, own reports up to the Force Commander in Zagreb and also to the Crisis Staff here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, did you have contacts with the Bosnian-Serb military officials from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your context with those officials did you complain to them about the effects of the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every time when we had a meeting with, let us say, with representatives of the Bosnian Serb Army -- I think we will come to the persons later -- we made out complaints given by the civil authorities within the enclave, what happened with the population, not only in providing food for them, but also on the medical side of the whole support for the people. In the beginning we supported the population as much as we could in combination with MSF, Medecins Sans Frontiere, by ambulances in the area, by giving them medicines, giving them medical care, pick up wounded persons or sick persons, bring them to the hospital in Srebrenica or, if that was not possible, to our own field dressing station. That was as of end of April also stopped. The same applied for, let us say, the normal daily living within the enclave. All those complaints we told several times when we had a meeting, we presented to the BSA to those representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was their reaction, Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you identify some of the persons in the Bosnian-Serb Army with whom you had contact and with whom you liaised on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sir. In the first place, and I met him in the first week when I arrived in Bosnia in Srebrenica, I met Colonel Vukovic. He was the so-called Liaison Officer between the Battalion and the Drina Corps Commander or the Drina Corps. He was also the Commander of one of Brigades, the Brigade in the southern part of the surroundings of Srebrenica. The second BSA representative which we met quite often was Major Nikolic. He was the Liaison Officer from the Bratunac Brigade, and the Bratunac Brigade was the Brigade in the northern area outside the enclave. He was the representative of that Brigade and he was also the LSO which we dealt often. Those two persons we met during not daily meetings, but sometimes a couple of times a week, sometimes even once a month when they liked to have a meeting and not when we liked to have a meeting. A third person I know as Petar. Petar is an interpreter which both just named officers used all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, during your contacts with Major Nikolic, did he ever express an opinion to you about his attitude towards the Bosnian Muslim population of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. Actually that was in one of the meetings what I can remember in February. We had always our meetings either on OP Echo, that is an observation post in the southern part of the enclave, or OP Papa in the northern part. This was on one of the occasions which I can remember in February in which he told me, you could see it on his face too, the hatred of the Muslim people, especially those who were Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.Pages 608 to 621. living in the enclave, and he said that he had a reason for that because half of his family had been murdered during the Second World War. Secondly, he told me that, in his opinion, all the Muslims should leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Thirdly, I think looking in those days at that moment to his face that he meant that, and that there was a quite some hatred in his eyes. Also in the words I must say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, you have mentioned that a number of Dutch soldiers were stationed inside the enclave of Srebrenica. Let me show you an exhibit which is a map of the enclave. It will be presented to you and then I would like to ask you some questions about it. Your Honours, we have copies as well for your Honours which I would ask the usher to please take up to the bench. Colonel Karremans, there should be a monitor in front of you, there should be that particular exhibit appearing in front of you on the monitor. Can you please point to the map and identify the locations where Dutch soldiers were stationed within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I can. If your Honours you look to the map you can see a dotted line in there with a C on top and a B, Bravo, in the south. What we did, and we took that over from the previous Battalion, was that we divided the area into two parts. The northern area was the responsibility of our C company, and the southern part of the area was the responsibility of the B COY, the Bravo company. We started off in January with eight observation posts from which we could see a great part of the area. In the beginning in January and February both companies had some observation posts. I start with the one here on top, OP Papa, that was the observation post I just was referring to when we had our meetings with BSA representatives. Then we have here OP Quebec and OP Romeo on the east side. We have OP November on the north. Those four, November, Papa, Quebec and Romeo, belonged to the C COY including the Alpha observation post. So that means five observation posts when we started off. The southern part of the enclave, OP Charlie, in the west, OP Echo here in the south and OP Fox Trot also in the south. That meant eight observation posts when I took it over. What I explained before, your Honours, is due to the convoy terror, if I may say so, and the lack of gasoline, diesel, we changed our mission, let us say, daily by daily, but especially our main mission working from observation posts and patrolling between observation posts and within the enclave to more observation posts and less patrolling by cars and later on only patrolling by foot. We decided to build more observation posts. We did that in contact with the BiH forces inside the enclave and we also discussed that with the BSA representatives. They all agreed to that, except observation post, Kilo over here, but I would like to come to that one later on, if I may. During our stay there we made OP Mike and OP Delta and OP Hotel, that is the old one, and at the end of our stay OP Hotel in the direct vicinity of the village of Srebrenica. There have been a lot of problems about OP Kilo, that was last one and Delta, because OP Kilo and Delta we projected those observation posts on smuggle routes, if I may say so, during our stay and also during the stay of both previous Battalions, we noticed there was a lot of smuggling between the safe area of Srebrenica and the safe area of Zepa and used a couple of routes from the southern part of the enclave in the southern direction to Zepa. That is why we put Delta and Kilo on those routes. From the Bosnian military side they had, let us say, quite some problems that we established those two observation posts. At the end we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Colonel Karremans, how many soldiers were stationed in each of those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started in January with, let us say, 10 soldiers per observation post, but after the end of April when the leave convoys did not return to Srebrenica and we made more observation posts and we did less patrolling or, let us say, it in another way, another kind of patrolling, we changed a little bit the manning of the observation posts and went to six in some cases and 10 in other cases. We had some observation posts with 10 persons just for observation and doing the patrols, and we had some observation posts with only six persons on it just for observation. In total at the end of our stay on 12 observation posts I had about 90 to 100 soldiers working day by day on the posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, had the Bosnian Serb blockade not taken place, what was the normal number of soldiers you would have had in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Battalion consisted of 780 soldiers. 180 were situated in the Tuzla area, one company, a large company I must say, and I had 600 soldiers, including 50 of the field dressing station, to my disposal within the enclave, 600, but at the end, let us say, in April about 150 to 180 did not return. So I had about 400, 420 soldiers at my disposal as of the end of April till the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of that 420 soldiers how many of those soldiers were infantry men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About half, 100 on the observation posts, about 100 for doing the patrols, especial patrolling in the enclave, along the borders of the enclave, for the guarding of both compounds in Srebrenica itself and in Potocari, and the other 200 soldiers were all for manning the three company staffs, the Battalion staff, for all the logistics and the field dressing station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So by the time the invasion started in July less than half of your available military personnel were infantry soldiers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Court what type of weaponry was available to your troops at the time the invasion started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Our government has chosen for a so-called light option, and the weaponry we had in those days were small arms, every soldier had his own arm, either a pistol or a light machine gun or a rifle. Then we had a light machine guns, guns on the observation posts and also on both compounds. We had the heavy machine guns on our armoured personnel carriers. Besides that we had six mortars, 81 millimetre. They were on the observation posts, let us say, on some of the observation posts. I had to my disposal anti-tank weapons, medium range and long range. Amongst them, for instance, the tow wide anti-tank systems and some small anti-tank weapons as well. I think that is what the main armament was of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the Bosnian Serb Army blockade of Srebrenica that started in April have any effect on the amount of ammunition or the quality of weaponry that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. That had already happened when we entered, let us say, the first Battalion, the enclave, because we had to work, I gave you that example, with small arms, our personal arms, which we took over from the previous Battalion and they took it over from the first Battalion. Those weapons, small arms, although they were maintained daily they were used a lot. The same applied for the anti-tank systems I had. Every half a year, for instance, a tow rocket should be in a test bed, you have to test it if it works well. I did not have that test equipment, so I could not rely on my anti-tank weapons. Another thing is when the Battalion came in, the first one, is that I had only 16 per cent of the ammunition I normally should have. That ammunition was after more than a year in bad circumstances as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, did General Mladic have good intelligence about what was happening in enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. In the first place he could notice by all the troops which he had around the enclave what was going on within the enclave. He could see what we were doing when we are patrolling, when we are leaving the compounds with vehicles or by patrols, when we were resupplying the observation posts. He knew everything that we did internally. Secondly, he was well aware of our supplies in the Battalion because he was the person or, le us say, his staff, were persons who refused, especially after the end of April, refused all our convoys. Those convoys which came in we used so-called loading papers on which you have to describe what you will have or receive. So they know exactly what was on supply in the enclave for our Battalion, food, medicines, spare parts, engineer equipment, etc. In the third place, he was well aware of what was going on in the enclave on both sides of the Battalion and also on the population and civil authorities. He mentioned that to me in one of the meetings I had with him, that he was well aware of what was going on in the enclave every day, every minute, by persons he had posted in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the Bosnian Serb invasion on the enclave started, did Bosnian Serb Army attack the outposts that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the invasion started in July 1995, did the BSA attack your observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That already started in June, 3rd June. I would like to recall or go back to the end of May when the air strikes were executed in the Pale area, with the result that I think over more than 300 UN soldiers were hijacked in those days. After that the problems in the safe areas Gorazde and Zepa with all the British and Ukrainian observation posts, and that happened also in the beginning of June. On 1st June I had to come to OP Echo, that is just at the southern part of the enclave, and there was a telephone call. We had a land line between the observation post Echo and one of the posts of the BSA, and we had a land line which we could use for making telephone calls and when we liked to have a meeting with them or they liked to have a meeting with us. I used the telephone and I got the interpreter on the other end, Petar, I referred to him, and the name of Vukovic asked me to consider leaving OP Echo. I asked him for a reason which he did not give me and that was it. I stated that I would not leave OP Echo at all. Two days later, and that was on 3rd June, in the early morning, I think it was about 9, all of a sudden after a warning of a couple of minutes the BSA attacked OP Echo with about 60 soldiers heavily armed with mortars, hand grenades, with anti-tank weapons, and the manning of the observation posts were all under fire to leave OP Echo. They happily succeeded without result leaving persons behind, but they left behind a lot of equipment. What they took with them were the vehicles, the communications systems, some personal stuff and weaponry. The rest was left on OP Echo. That was the first observation post we lost in the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Karremans, how many Dutch soldiers were manning OP Echo at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think 10 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please continue describing the attacks on the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that attack executed by what I stated before, by about 60 persons, leaving by the APC, with the APC, OP Echo, we did two things, actually three. In the first place, we made an immediate report for the high echelons what happened, what was going on. Secondly, we asked for a meeting with Colonel Vukovic or Nikolic to ask them what was going on, the purpose of that attack, that we would like to have back the observation post and that we would like to have back the equipment left behind on that observation post. The second thing we did immediately after losing that observation post was establishing OP Shera and OP Uniform, that is say, 200 to 300 metres north of OP Echo. That gave a remarkable reaction on the BSA because they, I think, did not expect that reaction. So, also we lost OP Echo. We had two observation posts nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the reaction of your Bosnian Serb Liaison Officer when you asked for the observation post back and for your equipment back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It took quite a while when we had a first meeting after the loss of OP Echo. I cannot remember when we had the first meeting after, let us say, 3rd June, but the reaction was that we could not get back the equipment and we could not get back the observation post at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there additional attacks on the observation posts prior to or during the invasion of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of the attacks on the observation posts, were Dutch soldiers taken prisoners by the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell us on which occasions they were taken prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. That happened, your Honours, on the start of, let us say, on 6th July that was already a month later. In the period between 3rd June, OP Echo, and 6th July, it was rather quiet in the area, also there was a tense situation, I must say, but it was really quiet, except one occasion somewhere in the middle of June, what happened in the vicinity of Srebrenica itself. On 6th July, in the morning, about 3 o'clock, the war started over there. It started in our area, the compound of Potocari, by shooting over the compound with some rockets. The attacks started in the southern part of the enclave, in the area of OP Fox Trot. That was on the Thursday, Thursday, 6th July. Those attacks were carried out, let us say, during six days. The first OP which has been attacked really by small arms, by mortars and by tanks was OP Fox Trot, that one on Thursday, on Friday and on Saturday, and it was Saturday, I think, by noonish or 1 o'clock that I ordered to retreat the manning of the OP and leave it during a pause of shootings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many men were stationed in OP Fox Trot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment -- seven men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Saturday, in the afternoon, when OP Fox Trot has been attacked for a third day, and I ask, I can remember, for a second time for close air support, things were going on rather quickly, because on Saturday and Sunday I lost quite some observation posts in the southern part of the enclave here. There were two possibilities for the soldiers on the observation posts -- actually, three possibilities: just leave the observation post and go back to the compound; secondly, stay as long as they could, making use of the defence walls, making use of the shelters within the observation post; thirdly, retreat from the observation post knowing that the BiH should make problems because they, not order us, but they thought that we should stay on the observation post and not retreat it or not leave them. There was another possibility just to end up, let us say, taken away by BSA forces. In most of the cases leaving the observation post, the last thing happened. The observation posts were attacked by BSA forces. They were encircled by forces, and the only thing the soldiers could do is hand over equipment, use their vehicles and they were sent, let us say, to Simici(?) or later on to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As a result of those actions by the BSA against the observation post, how many Dutch soldiers were taken into custody by the BSA and detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end there were 55 soldiers taken in custody and detained from seven or eight different observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those 55 soldiers were all infantry soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were all infantry soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If my mathematics are correct, that represented about 25 per cent of your infantrymen available in the compound at the time of the invasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know how many Bosnian Serb Army soldiers participated in the invasion of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you subsequently find out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because Mladic told me, General Mladic told me, at the end that he had quite some troops around the enclave of Srebrenica. Those were not the original troops around the enclave, but let us say fresh troops, fresh Brigades. He used one Brigade for the attack in the southern, from the southern direction, from south to north; he had another Brigade from east to the west and he had one Brigade in reserve north of Bratunac. Bratunac is the city somewhere over here. Actually, he told me he had three Brigades or Brigade sized units which he used too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many men are in a Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, but I think that in every Brigade there were about between 1,000 and 1500 soldiers with this heavy weaponry and other weaponry than we had in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to ask you specifically that question, Colonel Karremans, who type of weapons were available to the invading Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had all equipment from the former Yugoslavian Army -- at least what was left out of it. They had quite some artillery pieces. We have noticed those pieces already around the enclave during our stay over there. Sometimes they changed the position of those artillery pieces. Sometimes they changed the positions of mortars they have, heavy mortars, light mortars -- quite a lot, I must say. They had some main bell tanks, the old T55s, and even some new types which we have noticed and which they had used; some anti-aircraft vehicles which they did not use for anti-aircraft but for the attacks on the villages in the southern part of the enclave, I mean, in direct line and a lot of anti-tank weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they also have multiple rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a couple of multiple rocket systems, small ones, all on wheels, of which we have noticed at least three north of the compound of Potocari around the hills and he had, let us say, a larger multiple rocket system in the city of Bratunac which he used as well shelling the city of (indecipherable).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am looking at the clock; perhaps this is an appropriate time to recess for the day?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I share your view. This is a good moment to have a recess. We will stop the hearing for today and the Tribunal will resume tomorrow at 10 o'clock.
